Section 01The question: why can the polariton line be narrower?

A molecule in a condensed environment does not have a perfectly sharp optical transition. Its surroundings fluctuate, the molecular excitation displaces the surrounding vibrations, and the transition loses phase coherence. A cavity photon also has a finite lifetime. It is therefore tempting to assign a polariton the weighted average of a molecular linewidth and a cavity linewidth. The central observation in this paper is that this procedure misses an important piece of physics: the molecular part of a collective polariton does not experience the same effective fluctuation as one isolated molecule.

The calculation has two distinct tasks. First, determine the diagonal noise seen by an extended polariton. Second, retain the bath matrix elements that scatter a polariton into other polariton and dark states. The first task produces narrowing. The second explains why the upper and lower branches need not be equally narrow. A theory that only retains diagonal noise cannot, by itself, reproduce the full asymmetry.

This tutorial develops both mechanisms, the paper's practical linewidth interpolation, and the numerical absorption calculation. It uses the published main article and its Appendices A and B. The separate journal supplementary file was not retrieved; the hierarchy and rate derivations below are therefore written out as tutorial derivations rather than attributed to unseen supplementary equations. Equation numbers on this page are independent of the article's numbering.

Three levels of statement. Basis changes and projected matrix elements are algebraic identities. Gaussian line-shape limits require a specified diagonal-coupling model. The detuning-dependent linewidth formula in the article is an interpolation motivated by limits and tested against its HEOM calculations; it is not an exact identity of the full Hamiltonian.

Primary source: Ying, Mondal, and Huo, JCP 161, 064105 (2024); model in Sec. II, narrowing in Sec. III, linewidth interpolation and scattering in Sec. IV.

Section 02Units and the meaning of a linewidth

We use energies throughout. The cavity energy is Ec=ℏωc, a bath-mode energy is Eα=ℏωα, and the single-molecule light–matter coupling is v=ℏgc. The symbols λ, kBT, and γ denote energies; γ/ℏ is the Drude decay rate. A time-domain frequency is an energy divided by ℏ. This avoids mixing a value in meV with a rate in inverse femtoseconds.

For numerical conversions, ℏ≃658.21196 meV fs and kB≃0.08617333 meV K−1. A line's full width at half maximum is denoted W. Its Lorentzian half width is a=W/2. A population-decay rate, a coherence-decay rate, and a spectral FWHM are different quantities:

P(t)=P(0)e−kt,Ceg(t)=Ceg(0)e−kt/2,W=ℏk(population loss only).
(1)

If pure dephasing adds a coherence-decay rate γϕ, the FWHM is W=ℏk+2ℏγϕ. This factor of two will matter repeatedly. The article calls its spectral widths FWHM; below we explicitly audit the conversion from its Appendix A correlation function rather than relying on a symbol named “Gamma” to determine the convention.

Section 03Start with the full tensor-product space

Each molecule has a ground ket |gi⟩ and an excited ket |ei⟩. The cavity has photon-number kets |nc⟩, and every molecule has its own collection of harmonic bath modes. Before restricting excitation number, the space is

H=(⨂i=1Nspan{|gi⟩,|ei⟩})⊗Hc⊗(⨂i=1NHBi).
(2)

In the local ordered basis (|gi⟩,|ei⟩), the lowering operator, excited-state projector, and identity are

[σ^i−]=(0100),[P^i]=[σ^i+σ^i−]=(0001),[I^i]=(1001).
(3)

When P^i appears in a many-molecule formula, it means this matrix tensored with identities on every other factor. The same convention applies to a cavity operator and to a bath operator. Operators on different factors commute; raising and lowering operators on the same two-level molecule do not obey ordinary harmonic-boson algebra.

Section 04The Hamiltonian and the reorganization-energy convention

Let E0 be the relaxed molecular excitation energy and let ϵ=E0+λ be the vertical transition energy. With the photon zero-point constant omitted, the model is

H^=H^S⊗I^B+I^S⊗H^B+∑iP^i⊗B^i,H^S=ϵ∑iP^i+Eca^†a^+v∑i(σ^i+a^+σ^i−a^†),H^B=∑i,αEαb^iα†b^iα,B^i=∑αcα(b^iα+b^iα†).
(4)

The cα are energies. Independence means the bath state is a product over molecules and the cross-correlations vanish for different sites. Identical baths mean their mode energies, couplings, and temperatures have the same statistics. Independence does not mean that their fluctuations can be replaced by one identical random number acting on every molecule.

For one occupied molecule, complete the square mode by mode:

Eαb^†b^+cα(b^+b^†)=Eα(b^†+cαEα)(b^+cαEα)−cα2Eα,λ=∑αcα2Eα.
(5)

Thus the minimum of the excited surface is ϵ−λ=E0. Including +λ in ϵ and then adding another counterterm to the same Hamiltonian would count the shift twice. Conversely, comparing cavity resonance to E0 instead of ϵ changes the detuning convention.

Source: main article, Eqs. (1)–(9). The tutorial writes all spectral parameters as energies.

Section 05Ground and one-excitation sectors

Linear absorption from an electronically unexcited ensemble requires the ground state and one-excitation states. Define

|G⟩=|g1⋯gN⟩⊗|0c⟩,|c⟩=|g1⋯gN⟩⊗|1c⟩,|i⟩=|g1⋯ei⋯gN⟩⊗|0c⟩.
(6)

The ordered excited-sector basis is B1=(|c⟩,|1⟩,…,|N⟩). The system Hamiltonian and local bath projector become

[H^S]B1=(Ecvv⋯vvϵ0⋯0v0ϵ⋯0⋮⋮⋮⋱⋮v00⋯ϵ),P^i=|i⟩⟨i|.
(7)

This is an (N+1)-dimensional system block, not an (N+1)-dimensional description of the full system and its vibrations. HEOM retains the bath influence through auxiliary operators or auxiliary coherence kets. The restriction to one optical excitation does not eliminate bath memory.

Section 06Deriving the bright and dark basis

The cavity couples to a sum of molecular excitations. Normalize that sum to define the bright state:

|B⟩=1N∑i=1N|i⟩,⟨c|H^S|B⟩=Nv≡V.
(8)

The orthogonal complement of |B⟩ within the molecular sector has dimension N−1. Any orthonormal basis of it is a dark-state basis. For example, with site labels i=0,…,N−1, discrete Fourier kets give

|Dk⟩=1N∑i=0N−1e2πiki/N|i⟩,k=1,…,N−1,∑i=0N−1e2πiki/N=0.
(9)

The geometric-series identity proves that ⟨B|Dk⟩=0 and ⟨c|H^S|Dk⟩=0. “Dark” here means dark to this uniform cavity or optical coupling. It does not mean dynamically disconnected from local bath fluctuations.

In (|c⟩,|B⟩,|D1⟩,…), only the first two states form a coupled block; each dark state has energy ϵ.

Section 07Diagonalizing the polariton block without ambiguous angles

Set δ=Ec−ϵ, and choose V>0 by a fixed phase convention. The bright–cavity block is

[H^cB]=(EcVVϵ),E±=Ec+ϵ2±Ω2,Ω=δ2+4V2.
(10)

Here Ω is an energy splitting, not an angular frequency. Introduce the molecular probabilities w±, rather than relying on an inverse tangent whose branch may be ambiguous:

w+=12(1−δΩ),w−=12(1+δΩ),|+⟩=1−w+|c⟩+w+|B⟩,|−⟩=1−w−|c⟩−w−|B⟩.
(11)

At resonance, both branches are half matter and half photon. Far below the molecular transition, the cavity-like branch is LP and w−→0. Far above it, LP becomes molecular and w−→1. Checking these limits prevents a swapped Hopfield coefficient from propagating through every linewidth formula.

Section 08An explicit three-by-three transformation for two molecules

For N=2, define |D⟩=(|1⟩−|2⟩)/2. The columns of the following matrix are (|c⟩,|B⟩,|D⟩) written in B1=(|c⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩):

[U^]B1=(10001/21/201/2−1/2),U^†H^SU^=(Ec2v02vϵ000ϵ).
(12)

The bath projectors are not diagonal after this change of basis:

[P^1]cBD=12(000011011),[P^2]cBD=12(00001−10−11).
(13)

Consequently,

[H^SB]cBD=12(0000B^1+B^2B^1−B^20B^1−B^2B^1+B^2).
(14)

The sum of the two bath coordinates shifts the bright energy; their difference scatters the bright state into the dark state. Averaging the two coordinates first would erase the difference and remove a physical relaxation channel.

Section 09Bath matrix elements in the resonant polariton basis

Use the resonant ordered basis (|+⟩,|−⟩,|D⟩), with |±⟩=(|c⟩±|B⟩)/2. The two molecular projectors are

[P^1]=(1/4−1/41/(22)−1/41/4−1/(22)1/(22)−1/(22)1/2),[P^2]=(1/4−1/4−1/(22)−1/41/41/(22)−1/(22)1/(22)1/2).
(15)

These matrices answer three questions at once. Their diagonal polariton entries are 1/4, which controls diagonal noise. Their +,− entries generate interbranch scattering. Their polariton–dark entries generate scattering into the dark manifold. Squaring and summing the appropriate matrix elements is the correct starting point for a Golden-rule rate; a single “effective coupling” cannot stand in for all three processes.

Section 10The local bath correlation function

For a thermal harmonic oscillator, write n¯α=(eβEα−1)−1. Time evolution gives b^α(t)=b^αe−iEαt/ℏ. Since the only nonzero second moments are ⟨b^b^†⟩=n¯+1 and ⟨b^†b^⟩=n¯,

Cij(t)=⟨B^i(t)B^j(0)⟩B=δij∑αcα2[(n¯α+1)e−iEαt/ℏ+n¯αeiEαt/ℏ].
(16)

Define an energy-domain spectral density

JE(E)=π∑αcα2δ(E−Eα),C(t)=1π∫0∞dEJE(E)[coth⁡(βE2)cos⁡Etℏ−isin⁡Etℏ].
(17)

The real part determines symmetric fluctuations. The imaginary part is a quantum response contribution. Discarding it is not merely a harmless change of notation: it loses information tied to the unequal probabilities of emission and absorption of a bath quantum.

Section 11Drude decomposition and its thermal terms

The energy-domain Drude model is

JE(E)=2λγEE2+γ2,λ=1π∫0∞JE(E)EdE.
(18)

For t>0, evaluating the contour integral gives a Drude pole and Matsubara poles. A finite representation is

C(t)≃∑r=0Kcre−νrt/ℏ,ν0=γ,c0=λγ[cot⁡(βγ2)−i],νr=2πr/β,cr=4λγβνrνr2−γ2(r≥1).
(19)

This expansion is exact when the infinite sum is retained, away from coincident-pole parameterizations requiring a limiting treatment. Truncating it is an approximation separate from truncating the HEOM tiers. At high temperature, its slow Drude part has real amplitude 2λkBT. The ideal Drude quantum correlation has delicate short-time behavior; the finite high-temperature exponential is not an exact ultraviolet description of an unlimited Drude spectrum.

Section 12Project a local environment onto one polariton

Let |p⟩ be a normalized polariton whose molecular coefficient on site i is xi. The bath term diagonal in that state is obtained by taking a system-space matrix element:

B^p=⟨p|H^SB|p⟩S=∑i|xi|2B^i,Cp(t)=∑ij|xi|2|xj|2Cij(t).
(20)

For identical independent baths, only i=j survives. For a uniformly delocalized polariton, |xi|2=wp/N, hence

Cp(t)=wp2NC(t),λp=wp2Nλ.
(21)

The square is essential. The molecular probability is wp; the diagonal noise amplitude carries one factor of that probability, and its correlation carries two. At resonance, wp=1/2, so λp=λ/(4N). This projection is an exact matrix-element identity for the chosen uniform polariton; neglecting the other matrix elements afterward is an additional dynamical approximation.

Compare main Eq. (27). The explicit projectors above show what this reduction retains and what it omits.

Section 13What changes for localization or correlated environments?

The projection calculation generalizes immediately. Write qi=|xi|2/wp, so ∑iqi=1, and define the participation number by

Neff=1∑iqi2,Cp(t)=wp2NeffC(t)for identical independent baths.
(22)

Thus it is the number of significantly participating molecules, not necessarily the geometric count, that controls diagonal averaging. For equal weights and a bath covariance Cij=[(1−η)δij+η]C,

Cp(t)=wp2[η+1−ηN]C(t).
(23)

A completely common bath, η=1, does not gain a 1/N reduction. Positive correlations create a large-N floor. This is an illustrative covariance extension, not the independent-bath model benchmarked in the paper. It explains why the independence assumption must be stated when applying the scaling to a material.

Section 14From coherence to a line shape

For a selected transition with vertical energy Ev, the diagonal independent-boson model has coherence

L(t)=e−iEvt/ℏe−g(t),A(E)=1πℏRe∫0∞dteiEt/ℏL(t).
(24)

The bath average is Gaussian because the Hamiltonian is harmonic and the coupling is linear. Expanding the time-ordered exponential and collecting connected contractions leaves the second cumulant. For this diagonal model the result is not a weak-coupling truncation:

g(t)=1ℏ2∫0tds∫0sduC(u)=1ℏ2∫0t(t−u)C(u)du.
(25)

For a general multistate problem, system operators at different times need not commute; this simple scalar cumulant is then not an exact substitute for HEOM. That distinction separates the analytic line-shape discussion from the full HTC simulation.

Section 15Evaluate the double integral explicitly

For one correlation term ce−νt/ℏ, integrate the inner integral first and then the outer one:

∫0se−νu/ℏdu=ℏν(1−e−νs/ℏ),cℏ2∫0tdsℏν(1−e−νs/ℏ)=cν2(e−νt/ℏ+νtℏ−1).
(26)

Sum this result for every Drude/Matsubara term. The factor in parentheses vanishes quadratically at the origin; numerically it should be evaluated with expm1, or a short series, to avoid subtracting nearly equal floating-point numbers.

For the high-temperature real Drude correlation, define σ2=2λkBT and τB=ℏ/γ. The projected polariton coherence has

gp,R(t)=σp2γ2(e−t/τB+tτB−1),σp2=wp2Nσ2.
(27)

Section 16Slow and fast modulation: derive both scaling laws

Define κp=γ/σp. This compares the bath decorrelation time to the dephasing time set by its fluctuation amplitude. The words “slow” and “fast” are relative to that coherence, not just labels attached to a bath frequency in isolation.

For κp≪1, coherence is lost before the bath changes appreciably. Expand the exponential to second order:

gp,R(t)≃σp2t22ℏ2,Ap(E)≃12πσpexp⁡[−(E−Ep)22σp2],Wpslow=22ln⁡2σp∝N−1/2.
(28)

For κp≫1, most coherence survives through many bath-correlation times. The late-time exponential dominates the central line:

gp,R(t)≃σp2ℏγt+constant,Ap(E)≃1πap(E−Ep)2+ap2,ap=σp2γ,Wpfast=2ap∝N−1.
(29)

The same variance reduction produces different linewidth powers because a Gaussian width is proportional to the standard deviation, whereas a fast-modulation Lorentzian width is proportional to the variance. One should not mix the two limiting line shapes when combining broadening sources.

Section 17A width-convention checkpoint against Appendix A

The calculation above fixes all prefactors: with energy-domain CR(t)=2λkBTe−γt/ℏ, the long-time coherence-decay coefficient in energy units is a=2λkBT/γ. Therefore

1πℏRe∫0∞ei(E−Ev)t/ℏe−at/ℏdt=1πa(E−Ev)2+a2,W=2a.
(30)

There is a prefactor inconsistency to watch for in the printed Appendix A: the paragraph before Eq. (A7) writes the decay as g(t)≃Γt−iλt, but Eq. (A7) uses a Lorentzian with half width Γ/2. These two expressions cannot both use the same Γ as written. The N−1 scaling is unaffected. For implementation, use the actual time-domain decay or an explicitly measured FWHM instead of transferring a factor of two by symbol matching.

This page's analytic-scale calculator reports FWHM =2σp2/γ. Its separate paper-interpolation calculator uses the user-specified bare FWHM Wex in the published interpolation. Those are deliberately labeled as different constructions. A measured bare line need not itself be in the asymptotic fast regime even when the much narrower polariton is.

Inspect Appendix A, Eqs. (A4)–(A7) and Eqs. (29)–(31). This convention check is an explicit tutorial calculation, not a claim that a corrected journal version has been issued.

Section 18Increasing N can change which limit applies

At fixed molecular weight and fixed bath parameters,

κp=γNwp2λkBT,Ncross∼2wp2λkBTγ2.
(31)

A system that begins in the slow-modulation regime can enter the fast regime as its effective noise becomes smaller. Thus a finite-N trend resembling N−1/2 should not be extrapolated indefinitely while insisting that the regime label remains fixed.

There is a second change to consider: keeping v fixed increases the collective splitting as N, while keeping V=Nv fixed requires reducing v. Those choices leave the diagonal variance scaling intact at resonance but change the energies sampled by interbranch scattering. They need not produce the same total UP linewidth at large N.

Section 19Photon loss and why Lorentzian widths add

At optical energies, the thermal photon occupation is negligible for the parameters in the article. Introduce a photon population loss rate kc=Wc/ℏ, and a jump operator a^=|G⟩⟨c| in the retained sectors. Its dissipator is

D^cρ^=Wcℏ(a^ρ^a^†−12{a^†a^,ρ^}).
(32)

For a well-separated polariton with photon probability 1−wp, the leading projected optical-coherence factor is exp⁡[−(1−wp)Wct/(2ℏ)]. Multiplying this by another exponential adds coherence-decay exponents, hence adds Lorentzian FWHMs:

Wp≃(1−wp)Wc+Wpfast.
(33)

Multiplying a Gaussian coherence envelope by an exponential instead produces a Voigt-type line. Its FWHM is not the direct sum of a Gaussian FWHM and a Lorentzian FWHM. The distinction matters whenever the bare molecular spectrum remains slow or intermediate even though the cavity contribution is Markovian.

Section 20Recover the paper's detuning interpolation

The paper does not assert that projecting a single ideal polariton is sufficient at all detunings. Near the molecular limit, local bath coupling mixes nearly degenerate bright and dark states; the simple uniform-polariton picture ceases to describe the resolved molecular feature by itself. A practical formula must therefore recover the uncoupled molecular linewidth.

Write the published LP expression, main Eq. (34), using the LP molecular probability w=w−:

W~−=(1−w)Wc+w2(1−w)+w2/NWexN.
(34)

To understand its construction, start with the earlier expression containing w2/(1−w). It behaves sensibly near resonance but diverges as w→1. Adding w2/N to the denominator bounds the result and recovers the molecular endpoint. The limits are

w→0:W~−→Wc,w→1:W~−→Wex,w=12:W~−=Wc/2+Wex/(2N+1).
(35)

The last limit is worth checking explicitly. Main Eq. (31) gives a separate resonance estimate Wc/2+Wex/(2N), whereas substituting resonance into Eq. (34) gives Wc/2+Wex/(2N+1). The latter approaches the former at large N, with a molecular-term correction of order N−2; they are not identical at finite N. We retain Eq. (34) literally when plotting the paper's interpolation and do not silently make it equal to Eq. (31) or the projected cumulant.

The UP baseline, main Eq. (36), has exactly the same functional form after replacing w− by w+. Additional UP scattering is then included separately.

Source: main Eqs. (33)–(36). The algebraic endpoint evaluations here can be checked without any fit or simulation.

Section 21Derive the Golden-rule scattering factor

For an initial system eigenket |α⟩ and final eigenket |β⟩, perturbation theory in ∑iP^i⊗B^i gives a long-time transition rate proportional to the bath correlation Fourier transform. The independent baths eliminate cross terms between different i:

kα→β=1ℏ2∑i|⟨β|P^i|α⟩|2∫−∞∞dtei(Eα−Eβ)t/ℏC(t).
(36)

Substituting the oscillator correlation, the time integral gives 2πℏδ(Eα−Eβ−Eν) for emission. For a positive energy gap ΔE,

ℏkα→β=2JE(ΔE)[n¯(ΔE)+1]∑i|⟨β|P^i|α⟩|2.
(37)

The reverse absorption process replaces n¯+1 by n¯. Their ratio is e−βΔE. This is a population-rate result. Its contribution to optical FWHM equals ℏk, provided outgoing population loss produces half that rate of coherence damping and incoming coherences can be neglected in the secular approximation.

Section 22UP to LP and UP to dark states

For uniform molecules, the interbranch overlap on each site is −w+w−/N. Summing its squared magnitude gives

∑i|⟨−|P^i|+⟩|2=w+w−N,ℏk+→−=2w+w−NJE(Ω)[n¯(Ω)+1].
(38)

To sum all dark states, use their completeness projector rather than selecting a special Fourier basis:

∑d=1N−1|Dd⟩⟨Dd|=∑i|i⟩⟨i|−|B⟩⟨B|.
(39)

Its diagonal element on any site is 1−1/N. Hence

∑i,d|⟨Dd|P^i|+⟩|2=w+N−1N,ℏk+→D=2w+N−1NJE(E+−ϵ)[n¯(E+−ϵ)+1].
(40)

An individual dark channel is small; there are N−1 of them. Their sum need not vanish as N increases. This multiplicity is the important difference between diagonal averaging and decay into a manifold.

Section 23Why the branches are asymmetric—and when the argument fails

The paper's practical UP estimate adds the two emission channels to its baseline:

W~+=W+(0)+ℏk+→−+ℏk+→D.
(41)

The analogous LP channels require energy absorption. When the LP-to-dark and LP-to-UP gaps greatly exceed kBT, these are exponentially suppressed. UP can emit a quantum into the bath even at low temperature; LP cannot absorb an absent quantum. This explains the broader upper branch in the investigated regime.

It is not a theorem that LP scattering is zero at every detuning or temperature. When ϵ−E− becomes small, thermal upward scattering may matter. Likewise, at fixed collective splitting the total UP-to-dark rate approaches a finite value as N→∞. A diagonal 1/N dephasing law alone does not prove that the total UP linewidth vanishes.

The Golden-rule expressions also assume a perturbative bath-induced transition and a sufficiently well-defined energy gap. Overlapping peaks, strong vibronic mixing, structured resonances, or nonsecular dynamics require a direct calculation rather than a sum of independent decay widths.

Section 24A worked numerical example with two separate predictions

Take N=4, V=136.2 meV, δ=0, λ=30 meV, γ=24.8 meV, T=300 K, and Wc=44.15 meV. These are consistent with the scale of the article's detuning example. The splitting is 272.4 meV, kBT≃25.852 meV, and both molecular probabilities are 1/2.

The projected reorganization energy and noise amplitude are

λp=1.875 meV,σp=2λpkBT≃9.846 meV,κp≃2.519.
(42)

The projected fast-limit FWHM is about 7.82 meV before cavity loss. The paper's interpolation instead uses the supplied bare FWHM, Wex=76.5 meV, giving

W~−=44.15/2+76.5/9=30.575 meV.
(43)

These numbers are not supposed to be identical: one is an asymptotic diagonal-bath estimate; the other is the empirical interpolation with a measured bare linewidth. The calculator below keeps the two outputs visibly separate and adds the UP Golden-rule estimate only to the interpolation baseline.

Section 25Explore ensemble size, detuning, and linewidth conventions

All energies in this calculator are in meV. It assumes independent identical baths, uniform coupling, and a supplied collective coupling V. Changing N while keeping V fixed therefore changes the single-molecule coupling to V/N. No input is a prediction of the complete HEOM spectrum.

Section 26The HEOM state and its equation

Represent each local correlation by K+1 exponentials. The hierarchy label is an integer array n=(nir). Its tier is ∑irnir; ρ^0 is the physical reduced density operator. Higher-tier auxiliary density operators store bath-memory information and are not separate physical density matrices.

Using energy-valued νr and unscaled auxiliaries, a standard convention is

ρ^˙n=−iℏ[H^S,ρ^n]−1ℏ∑irnirνrρ^n+D^cρ^n−iℏ∑ir[P^i,ρ^n+eir]−iℏ∑irnir(crP^iρ^n−eir−cr∗ρ^n−eirP^i).
(44)

A hard cutoff sets auxiliaries above a maximum tier to zero. That is only one closure choice. Convergence in tier, number of bath terms, propagation timestep, and spectral window must be checked separately. Adding the same Markovian cavity dissipator to every auxiliary is distinct from modifying the molecular correlation function.

The hierarchy written here assumes the real decay energies of the Drude/Matsubara representation. More general complex exponential pairs require appropriate conjugate-channel bookkeeping. The linked symHEOM note develops the compression problem separately.

Section 27Linear spectroscopy can propagate auxiliary coherence kets

For a cold electronic ground state and a thermal uncoupled bath, an optical excitation creates an operator of the form |u⟩⟨G|. Because P^i|G⟩=0 and H^S|G⟩=0, this sector closes:

ρ^n(μ)=|un⟩⟨G|,|u˙n⟩=−iℏH^S|un⟩−1ℏ∑irnirνr|un⟩−Wc2ℏ|c⟩⟨c|un⟩−iℏ∑irP^i|un+eir⟩−iℏ∑irnircrP^i|un−eir⟩.
(45)

The terms involving right multiplication by P^i vanish, and the photon recycling term vanishes in this optical-coherence block. This does not justify omitting recycling when propagating excited populations. It is a block-specific simplification.

A scaled auxiliary |u~n⟩=|un⟩/∏irnir!|cr|nir replaces upward coefficients by (nir+1)|cr| and downward coefficients by crnir/|cr|. The provided teaching script uses this scaling and a hard tier cutoff.

Section 28Construct the initial optical ket and detected correlation

For identical aligned molecular dipoles, the paper normalizes the dipole by 1/N. With a scalar dipole magnitude absorbed into the signal normalization,

μ^+=1N∑i|i⟩⟨G|,|u0(0)⟩=μ^+|G⟩=|B⟩,|un≠0(0)⟩=0.
(46)

The detected correlation is Cμ(t)=⟨B|u0(t)⟩. A cavity-driven probe instead initializes and detects |c⟩. The poles can be related, but residues and intensities differ; an absorption signal must specify which dipole or field couples to the experiment.

For a genuinely correlated thermal initial state, applying the optical operator only to the zeroth tier generally loses initial system–bath correlations. Apply it to the entire equilibrium hierarchy. The ground-state simplification above is justified here by the large electronic excitation energy and the projector coupling that leaves the electronic ground-state bath undisplaced.

Section 29A reproducible numerical workflow

Construct the system matrix and all projector diagonals in the stated basis. Generate every hierarchy label up to the chosen tier and precompute its raised/lowered neighbors. Store the scaled auxiliary coherence kets in an array with shape “hierarchy states by N+1.” At each derivative evaluation, apply the Hamiltonian, tier damping, cavity optical damping, and upward/downward terms.

For absorption, save only ⟨B|u0(t)⟩ unless other diagnostics are needed. Multiply by any chosen window only after documenting it, then Fourier transform with the +iEt/ℏ convention. The finite-time frequency resolution is on the order of 2πℏ/tmax; zero padding interpolates a spectrum but does not improve that physical resolution.

The teaching implementation propagates a conventional small hierarchy, not the article's production implementation or the symmetry-reduced solver. It includes a scalar cumulant reference, so a decoupled one-molecule optical coherence can be checked independently of the hierarchy code.

Section 30Reading the numerical figures without over-extrapolating

Figure 1 compares ensemble-size changes with fixed single-molecule coupling and fixed collective splitting, and contrasts bath-memory regimes. The linewidth powers are evidence for the diagonal-noise mechanism within those finite systems. They are not a reason to discard interbranch scattering when extrapolating a different large-system sequence.

Figures 2 and 3 vary detuning and compare numerical widths to the linewidth formulas. When evaluating the comparison, inspect both the peak positions and whether the two peaks are sufficiently separated for a stable FWHM extraction. A dip between overlapping peaks can make a naively measured half-maximum width ambiguous. Appendix B varies cavity loss; as loss grows, resolved polariton peaks can disappear even though the Hermitian Hamiltonian still has two eigenvalues.

The main numerical setup uses a Drude bath and a mixed HEOM–Lindblad treatment. It is not a derivation of a universal linewidth formula for any correlated disorder, multimode dispersion, or arbitrarily structured spectral density.

Source: Fig. 1, Figs. 2–3 and Sec. V, and Appendix B.

Section 31Checks that distinguish numerical and physical convergence

A correct change of basis preserves eigenvalues and P^i2=P^i. The projector sum over dark states must equal the molecular identity minus the bright projector. Those are algebraic tests. A hierarchy propagation should then be tested against the bath-free system and the independent-boson monomer limit. Those are dynamical tests.

Next increase hierarchy depth, thermal-pole count, and propagation accuracy independently. Finally increase the observation time and examine sensitivity to the Fourier window. A low imaginary part in an extracted spectrum or a plausible narrowing trend is not a substitute for these checks. Optical coherences are complex transition operators; their auxiliary kets need not have unit norm.

The calculator is a comparison of analytic scales, not a certificate that all its input combinations satisfy strong coupling, high temperature, weak interbranch scattering, or a fast-modulation limit. Its warnings identify some obvious failures; they do not replace a regime analysis.

Section 32Exercises with worked solutions

1. Why does the vertical energy contain +λ?

For each occupied bath mode, completing the square lowers the minimum by cα2/Eα. Summing gives a lowering of λ, so a vertical energy E0+λ produces a relaxed gap E0. Adding a second identical counterterm would shift the physical model.

2. Verify the dimer dark state by matrix multiplication.

In (|c⟩,|1⟩,|2⟩), |D⟩=(0,1,−1)T/2. The first row of the Hamiltonian gives v/2−v/2=0; the other rows give ϵ|D⟩. Therefore it has no cavity coupling but remains a legitimate molecular eigenstate.

3. Calculate λ_eff for N = 100 at resonance.

The molecular probability is w=1/2. The projected coupling coefficients are cα/(2N), so λeff=λ/(4N)=λ/400. This is a diagonal projection; dark-state decay has not been included.

4. Find the noise reduction for nonuniform weights.

Let the normalized molecular probabilities be (1/2,1/4,1/4). Their squared sum is 3/8, giving Neff=8/3. A half-matter state therefore has λp=λ(1/4)(3/8)=3λ/32, not λ/12.

5. What is the large-N floor for 10% common noise?

With η=0.1, the variance factor is w2[0.1+0.9/N]. It approaches 0.1w2, so the independent-bath narrowing does not continue to zero. The covariance is a model assumption and should be measured or justified for an application.

6. Derive the Gaussian FWHM rather than identifying it with σ.

Set exp⁡[−x2/(2σ2)]=1/2. The two roots are x=±σ2ln⁡2. Their separation is 2σ2ln⁡2. Thus a standard deviation and a FWHM differ even before discussing polariton fractions.

7. A coherence decays as exp(−0.01 t). What is its FWHM?

With ℏ=1, the HWHM is 0.01, and the FWHM is 0.02. If the decay came entirely from population loss, the corresponding population-decay rate would also be 0.02. This is the direct transform used in the width-convention audit.

8. Evaluate main Eq. (34) at resonance.

Substitute w=1/2. The molecular term is [(1/4)/(1/2+1/(4N))](Wex/N)=Wex/(2N+1). The photon term is Wc/2. This does not equal Wc/2+Wex/(2N) exactly at finite N, but tends to it as N increases.

9. Sum the UP-to-dark overlap for N = 4 at resonance.

The sum over all sites and all three dark states is w+(N−1)/N=(1/2)(3/4)=3/8. Multiplication by 2JE(ΔE)(n¯+1) gives the energy-valued Golden-rule rate. There is no extra factor of three afterward; the dark-state sum is already included.

10. Compare upward and downward scattering across a 100 meV gap at 300 K.

The ratio is e−100/25.852≃0.0209. Upward scattering is small, not identically zero. For a 10 meV gap the ratio is about 0.679, so neglecting absorption would be much less defensible.

11. Does a fixed collective splitting make all UP broadening vanish as N grows?

No. The direct interbranch overlap scales as 1/N, but the summed UP-to-dark overlap approaches w+. At fixed gaps and bath parameters, that summed rate can approach a nonzero floor while diagonal pure dephasing continues to decrease.

12. Why can optical HEOM use kets but population HEOM cannot simply discard recycling?

For |u⟩⟨G|, right multiplication by P^i vanishes and a^|u⟩⟨G|a^†=0. For |c⟩⟨c|, the same jump gives |G⟩⟨G|, which is required to preserve total probability.

13. Estimate the slow-to-fast crossover for a half-matter state.

Setting κp=1 gives Ncross=λkBT/(2γ2). This is only a scale estimate, not a sharp phase transition. Near the crossover, evaluate the full time integral instead of using either limiting FWHM.

14. Does doubling the zero-padding length double spectral resolution?

No. It produces more plotted frequency samples of the same finite-time information. Resolving a narrower line requires a longer converged correlation function, not merely more zeros appended to it.

Section 33Teaching code, scope, and further reading

Download the NumPy teaching script. The file contains projector tests, the paper's interpolation, detailed-balance rates, scalar cumulant line shapes, a direct absorption transform, and a small conventional scaled optical-coherence HEOM with a hard cutoff. It uses dimensionless energies and times with ℏ=1 for its propagation examples; the browser calculator uses meV and kelvin. The distinction is stated in the script's documentation.

python motional_narrowing_teaching.py --test
python motional_narrowing_teaching.py --demo --output narrowing_demo.csv

The demonstration saves a complex coherence trace and a second CSV containing its directly transformed spectrum. That spectrum explicitly includes an exponential window with rate 0.04 in the script's dimensionless units; this introduces additional broadening and is not a fitted physical decay. The demonstration is a reproducible small model, not a digitization or regeneration of the published figures. The script is intentionally readable rather than optimized for large ensembles. For the separate hierarchy-compression problem, continue to the symmetry-adapted HEOM Deep Dive. For spectral coherence signatures rather than just linewidths, see the PNAS Deep Dive.

Primary citation: Wenxiang Ying, M. Elious Mondal, and Pengfei Huo, “Theory and quantum dynamics simulations of exciton-polariton motional narrowing,” The Journal of Chemical Physics 161, 064105 (2024), DOI: 10.1063/5.0225387. The mathematical extensions and numerical examples on this page should be read with their stated assumptions; they are not additional published benchmark results.
